newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ruling PRI lashes out at U.S. Congress.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ruling PRI lashes out at U.S. Congress.

text.p: Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) on Friday lashed out at the U.S. Congress for trying to roll back President Bill Clinton's certification of Mexico's anti-drug efforts.
Humberto Roque Villanueva, outspoken leader of the party that has ruled Mexico for 68 years, accused U.S. lawmakers of trying to destabilise the United States' southern neighbour.
"Some members of the United States Congress are trying to destabilise our country," Roque Villanueva told reporters.

A U.S. House of Representatives committee on Thursday voted to overturn Clinton's finding last week that Mexico was cooperating in the drug war, but voted to waive imposition of sanctions. The full House was expected to vote on the measure.

The move stung Mexico, which has said it is doing what it can to fight the multi-billion dollar drugs trade but was rocked by a series of of scandals in recent weeks including the arrest of its top anti-drug official on charges he was in the payroll of a top drug lord.
Clinton and his drug czar Barry McCaffrey on Friday defended the administration's certification of Mexico and said they opposed Congress' efforts to reverse it.
Clinton "takes strong issue with the House committee," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry told reporters.
McCaffrey said nationalistic attitudes in Mexico hindered cooperation with the United States on the drug front.

"On the other side of the fence, there is an intense nationalistic debate, a crescendo of disapproval and antipathy toward the United States, isolating and constraining what we say are these incredibly brave Mexican patriots in charge in their own country and limiting their options to cooperate with the United States," McCaffrey told reporters.
"There's a problem on both sides of the border with that."

But the administrations' efforts did not stop a war of words that erupted on Thursday when Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat, suggested the United States would only get full anti-drug cooperation from Mexico without the long-ruling PRI.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo warned the U.S. Congress later that day that its moves to roll back certification were treading on Mexico's internal affairs.

"The Mexican government will act with all its might to defend the dignity and the sovereignty of all Mexicans...(I hope) this issue is resolved without forcing us to react vigorously," Zedillo told representatives from 13 Latin American countries in the Caribbean resort of Cancun.
And Roque Villanueva responded directly to Sen. Hollings on Friday by accusing him of interfering in Mexican affairs.

"In a clear aggression to our sovereignty, some suggest it would be better to provoke a crisis in Mexico," he said. "Mexico is not to blame for our geographical position next to the world's largest drug market," he added.
